column1: The statement is hawkish and risk-averse: it emphasizes elevated inflation from pandemic-induced supply and demand imbalances and energy shocks, now amplified by Russia’s invasion of Ukraine—factors the literature links to cost-push pressures that raise inflation while dampening growth (sticky-price and imperfect-information models; energy price surges negatively impact growth; COVID-19 supply-chain shocks). The Fed’s 75 bp rate hike, higher administered rates (IORB/ON RRP), and balance sheet runoff caps are consistent with Taylor-rule style responses and modern operating frameworks (Goodfriend, 2002; Bernanke–Mihov policy-shock identification), and the Committee’s “strong commitment” to 2% aims to anchor expectations in line with the New Keynesian Phillips Curve and inflation-forecast–targeting ideas (Svensson and Woodford, 2005; average inflation bias). Recent research on inflation-at-risk highlights a right-skew to inflation outcomes in this period, justifying a forceful stance but increasing near-term downside risk to activity; pandemic weighting evidence (e.g., Israel) also points to persistent, broad-based price pressures rather than narrow relative price shifts. Robust job gains provide a partial offset, but on net the tone is negative for near-term macro momentum and financial conditions. sentiment score = -0.20
